FinOps is unit economics, not cost cutting, the argument in one line. Allocation architecture precedes optimization; unattributed spend is unmanageable spend.
Commitment strategy is a utilization game: 90%+ coverage without idle waste.
Architectural cost reviews redesign expensive paths before deployment, not after invoices.

finOps is unit economics, not cost cutting fails, when it fails, in one specific place: lift-and-shift economics: estates migrated without unit-cost telemetry, so the savings case quietly erodes while the bill grows more opaque.

Against finOps is unit economics, not cost cutting, the strongest counter-case is worth naming: the unit-economics thesis can excuse under-provisioning that costs more in incidents than it saves in compute. FinOps is a balance, not a crusade.

In delivery, finOps is unit economics, not cost cutting becomes a specific discipline: infrastructure is treated as a product: versioned, observable, costed, and handed to your team with runbooks rather than folklore.
